title: Evolution Evidence and Life History Core Test
description: Core practice for fossils, common ancestry, shared structures, and evidence across time.

questions.prompt: What does the fossil record provide evidence about?
questions.questionText: What does the fossil record provide evidence about?
options: past life and changes in organisms over time
how organisms choose traits instantly
why all rocks contain DNA
why every species is unchanged forever
questions.correctAnswer: past life and changes in organisms over time
questions.explanation: Fossils preserve clues about organisms that lived in the past.

questions.prompt: A fossil is found in a deeper rock layer than another fossil. What is often a reasonable first inference?
questions.questionText: A fossil is found in a deeper rock layer than another fossil. What is often a reasonable first inference?
options: The deeper fossil must be alive now.
The deeper fossil may be older, depending on the rock history.
The deeper fossil has no scientific value.
Depth always shows the fossil is younger.
questions.correctAnswer: The deeper fossil may be older, depending on the rock history.
questions.explanation: Relative rock layers can help scientists infer age patterns when the layers are undisturbed.

questions.prompt: Which evidence can support common ancestry?
questions.questionText: Which evidence can support common ancestry?
options: different classroom labels
the color of a notebook
similar bone patterns in different organisms
one animal being larger than another
questions.correctAnswer: similar bone patterns in different organisms
questions.explanation: Shared structural patterns can be evidence that organisms share ancestry.

questions.prompt: A whale flipper, bat wing, and human arm have similar bone arrangements. Which claim does this evidence support?
questions.questionText: A whale flipper, bat wing, and human arm have similar bone arrangements. Which claim does this evidence support?
options: The organisms are the same species.
Bones are not useful evidence.
All three structures have identical functions.
These organisms may share common ancestry.
questions.correctAnswer: These organisms may share common ancestry.
questions.explanation: Similar underlying structures with different functions can suggest common ancestry.

questions.prompt: Which model best represents evidence for life changing over time?
questions.questionText: Which model best represents evidence for life changing over time?
options: older fossils -> transitional patterns -> newer fossils
newer fossils -> no past life -> no evidence
one fossil -> every answer
organism choice -> instant fossil
questions.correctAnswer: older fossils -> transitional patterns -> newer fossils
questions.explanation: Patterns across older and newer fossils can show change over time.

questions.prompt: A student says, "One fossil proves the whole history of a group." What is the best correction?
questions.questionText: A student says, "One fossil proves the whole history of a group." What is the best correction?
options: One fossil always proves every detail.
Scientists look for patterns across many fossils and other evidence.
Fossils cannot be compared.
Evidence from rocks is never useful.
questions.correctAnswer: Scientists look for patterns across many fossils and other evidence.
questions.explanation: Strong scientific explanations use multiple lines of evidence.

questions.prompt: A rock layer contains marine shell fossils in a desert region. What claim can this support?
questions.questionText: A rock layer contains marine shell fossils in a desert region. What claim can this support?
options: Shells prove the desert is underwater today.
Fossils cannot show past environments.
The environment in that area may have been different in the past.
The shells must be plastic.
questions.correctAnswer: The environment in that area may have been different in the past.
questions.explanation: Marine fossils can show that the past environment differed from today.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best support that two species are closely related?
questions.questionText: Which evidence would best support that two species are closely related?
options: different names in a textbook
one species living farther north
one species being photographed first
similar DNA patterns and similar body structures
questions.correctAnswer: similar DNA patterns and similar body structures
questions.explanation: Multiple shared evidence patterns strengthen a relatedness claim.

questions.prompt: A diagram compares embryo stages of several vertebrates and shows early similarities. What can this evidence help support?
questions.questionText: A diagram compares embryo stages of several vertebrates and shows early similarities. What can this evidence help support?
options: related developmental patterns among organisms
that all adult organisms are identical
that embryos are rocks
that development never changes
questions.correctAnswer: related developmental patterns among organisms
questions.explanation: Embryo similarities can be one line of evidence for relatedness.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a fossil from a living organism?
questions.questionText: Which statement best distinguishes a fossil from a living organism?
options: A fossil is always currently alive.
A fossil is preserved evidence of past life, not the living organism itself.
A fossil is a type of weather.
A fossil cannot be evidence.
questions.correctAnswer: A fossil is preserved evidence of past life, not the living organism itself.
questions.explanation: Fossils preserve traces or remains of past organisms.

questions.prompt: A sequence of horse fossils shows gradual changes in toe structure across rock layers. Which claim is best supported?
questions.questionText: A sequence of horse fossils shows gradual changes in toe structure across rock layers. Which claim is best supported?
options: Every individual horse changed its toes during life.
Fossils show no patterns.
Some body structures changed in that lineage over time.
Rock layers are unrelated to time.
questions.correctAnswer: Some body structures changed in that lineage over time.
questions.explanation: A fossil sequence can show population-level changes across long time spans.

questions.prompt: Which data pattern best supports common ancestry among three organisms?
questions.questionText: Which data pattern best supports common ancestry among three organisms?
options: They live in three different habitats.
They are drawn on the same page.
They have different adult sizes.
They share many DNA similarities and a similar limb-bone pattern.
questions.correctAnswer: They share many DNA similarities and a similar limb-bone pattern.
questions.explanation: Independent similarities in DNA and anatomy can support common ancestry.

questions.prompt: A student says, "Similar function always means common ancestry." Which example shows why that is too simple?
questions.questionText: A student says, "Similar function always means common ancestry." Which example shows why that is too simple?
options: Bird wings and insect wings both fly but have very different structures.
All wings are drawn with arrows.
Birds have feathers.
Insects are small.
questions.correctAnswer: Bird wings and insect wings both fly but have very different structures.
questions.explanation: Similar function alone is weaker than similar underlying structure and other evidence.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists compare fossils with modern organisms?
questions.questionText: Why do scientists compare fossils with modern organisms?
options: to avoid using evidence
to identify patterns of similarity, difference, and change over time
to prove all organisms are identical
to turn fossils into living organisms
questions.correctAnswer: to identify patterns of similarity, difference, and change over time
questions.explanation: Comparisons help connect past and present life.

questions.prompt: Which fossil discovery would most improve a model of transition between two groups?
questions.questionText: Which fossil discovery would most improve a model of transition between two groups?
options: a rock with no preserved structures
a fossil from an unknown layer with no details
a fossil with a mix of traits found in older and newer groups
a drawing with no measurements
questions.correctAnswer: a fossil with a mix of traits found in older and newer groups
questions.explanation: A fossil with mixed traits can help fill a gap in a change-over-time model.

questions.prompt: A fossil jaw has tooth shapes similar to a modern herbivore. What is a careful inference?
questions.questionText: A fossil jaw has tooth shapes similar to a modern herbivore. What is a careful inference?
options: The fossil organism was identical to the modern herbivore.
Teeth cannot provide evidence.
The organism chose new teeth because it needed them.
The fossil organism may have eaten plant material, but more evidence would strengthen the claim.
questions.correctAnswer: The fossil organism may have eaten plant material, but more evidence would strengthen the claim.
questions.explanation: Tooth structure can support feeding inferences, but careful science avoids overclaiming.

questions.prompt: A model groups organisms by shared structures. What would make the model stronger?
questions.questionText: A model groups organisms by shared structures. What would make the model stronger?
options: including DNA, fossil, and developmental evidence when available
removing all evidence
using only organism names
choosing the largest organism as ancestor
questions.correctAnswer: including DNA, fossil, and developmental evidence when available
questions.explanation: Multiple evidence types make ancestry models stronger.

questions.prompt: Which claim goes beyond the evidence if only one footprint fossil is found?
questions.questionText: Which claim goes beyond the evidence if only one footprint fossil is found?
options: An organism passed through this area.
The species definitely lived in large herds every year.
The organism had a foot that left a mark.
The rock preserved a trace of past life.
questions.correctAnswer: The species definitely lived in large herds every year.
questions.explanation: One footprint can support presence, but not detailed herd behavior by itself.

questions.prompt: A fossil layer has many fern fossils and no cactus fossils. A newer layer has dry-land plant fossils. Which claim is reasonable?
questions.questionText: A fossil layer has many fern fossils and no cactus fossils. A newer layer has dry-land plant fossils. Which claim is reasonable?
options: Plants cannot fossilize.
The older layer must be younger.
The local environment may have changed over time.
All plants vanished from Earth.
questions.correctAnswer: The local environment may have changed over time.
questions.explanation: Changes in fossil types across layers can suggest environmental change.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best uses both similarities and differences?
questions.questionText: Which explanation best uses both similarities and differences?
options: Only differences matter.
Only identical organisms can be related.
Similarities are never evidence.
Shared structures can support relatedness, while differences can show later changes in form or function.
questions.correctAnswer: Shared structures can support relatedness, while differences can show later changes in form or function.
questions.explanation: Evolution evidence often depends on patterns of both similarity and difference.

questions.prompt: A student says, "Fossils are useless because they are incomplete." What is the best response?
questions.questionText: A student says, "Fossils are useless because they are incomplete." What is the best response?
options: Fossils are incomplete, but patterns across many fossils can still provide strong evidence.
Incomplete evidence can never be useful.
Scientists never compare fossils.
Only living organisms can be evidence.
questions.correctAnswer: Fossils are incomplete, but patterns across many fossils can still provide strong evidence.
questions.explanation: Science often uses partial evidence carefully and combines many lines of evidence.

questions.prompt: Which question would best evaluate a common-ancestry claim?
questions.questionText: Which question would best evaluate a common-ancestry claim?
options: Which organism is more famous?
Do the organisms share detailed structures, DNA patterns, or developmental features?
Which organism has the shortest name?
Can the organisms be drawn in color?
questions.correctAnswer: Do the organisms share detailed structures, DNA patterns, or developmental features?
questions.explanation: Common ancestry claims need relevant evidence, not popularity or labels.

questions.prompt: A fossil shows limb bones where a modern species has a reduced structure. Which claim could this support?
questions.questionText: A fossil shows limb bones where a modern species has a reduced structure. Which claim could this support?
options: Structures never change.
Modern organisms have no history.
A structure may have changed size or function over time.
Reduced structures cannot be evidence.
questions.correctAnswer: A structure may have changed size or function over time.
questions.explanation: Changed or reduced structures can provide evidence about evolutionary history.

questions.prompt: Which statement avoids overclaiming from fossil evidence?
questions.questionText: Which statement avoids overclaiming from fossil evidence?
options: The fossils prove every exact event.
No conclusion can ever be made.
The newest fossil created the oldest fossil.
The fossils support a possible change-over-time pattern, but more evidence could refine the model.
questions.correctAnswer: The fossils support a possible change-over-time pattern, but more evidence could refine the model.
questions.explanation: Strong scientific reasoning matches the strength of the evidence.

questions.prompt: A fossil series shows body armor becoming less common over time in a lineage. What does the pattern directly show?
questions.questionText: A fossil series shows body armor becoming less common over time in a lineage. What does the pattern directly show?
options: a change in a trait pattern across time
why every individual changed during life
that environments never matter
that fossils are not evidence
questions.correctAnswer: a change in a trait pattern across time
questions.explanation: Trait patterns across fossil layers can show change over time.

questions.prompt: Which model best shows common ancestry?
questions.questionText: Which model best shows common ancestry?
options: one straight line saying every organism becomes stronger
branching lines from shared ancestors to related groups
a circle showing no change
a list sorted only by body size
questions.correctAnswer: branching lines from shared ancestors to related groups
questions.explanation: Branching models represent related groups sharing ancestors.

questions.prompt: A scientist compares two fossils but does not know their rock-layer ages. What evidence is missing?
questions.questionText: A scientist compares two fossils but does not know their rock-layer ages. What evidence is missing?
options: the fossil color only
the name of the museum gift shop
time-order evidence that helps place fossils in sequence
whether the fossils are popular
questions.correctAnswer: time-order evidence that helps place fossils in sequence
questions.explanation: Age or relative order helps interpret change over time.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best connects fossils to evolution?
questions.questionText: Which explanation best connects fossils to evolution?
options: Fossils show that populations never change.
Fossils replace all other evidence.
Fossils are unrelated to past life.
Fossils provide evidence of past organisms and patterns of change across long time spans.
questions.correctAnswer: Fossils provide evidence of past organisms and patterns of change across long time spans.
questions.explanation: The fossil record is a major line of evidence for evolution.

questions.prompt: A student builds a claim from fossils, DNA, and body-structure comparisons. Why is this stronger than using fossils alone?
questions.questionText: A student builds a claim from fossils, DNA, and body-structure comparisons. Why is this stronger than using fossils alone?
options: Different kinds of evidence can support the same explanation from multiple directions.
More evidence always means no reasoning is needed.
DNA removes the need to interpret fossils carefully.
Body structures are never useful.
questions.correctAnswer: Different kinds of evidence can support the same explanation from multiple directions.
questions.explanation: Converging evidence makes explanations stronger.

questions.prompt: Which final summary best shows understanding of evolution evidence?
questions.questionText: Which final summary best shows understanding of evolution evidence?
options: One fossil tells every detail.
Patterns in fossils, structures, embryos, and DNA help explain common ancestry and change over time.
Similar function is the only evidence needed.
Evolution evidence is not based on patterns.
questions.correctAnswer: Patterns in fossils, structures, embryos, and DNA help explain common ancestry and change over time.
questions.explanation: This summary connects several evidence types to common ancestry and change over time.
